title: Aspen Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Aspen wells have a 127 ft median depth, 15 gpm median yield, and estimated finished costs of $14,300-$24,700.
h1: What Aspen Wells Cost, Yield, and Require
intro_html:
Buying mountain property in Aspen means looking past the view and checking the well record. Within 5 miles of Aspen, Colorado, DWR records include 1,648 permitted wells, with 920 reporting total depth and 291 reporting pump yield. The numbers point to fractured-bedrock drilling where nearby results are useful, but no single well guarantees the same outcome.

Most permitted wells serve domestic or household use, and the records include properties around Woody Creek, Snowmass Village, Snowmass, and other nearby areas. Use this page to frame a driller’s bid, identify questions for the seller, and plan septic, access, and building work.

sections.heading: Aspen well depths vary with mountain bedrock
sections.html:
The median recorded well depth near Aspen is 127 feet. The middle half runs from 63 to 260 feet, so a proposed well near the median is not unusual, but a bid should allow for meaningful variation. Forty percent of recorded wells are under 100 feet, while 38% fall between 100 and 300 feet. Another 20% are between 300 and 600 feet, and 2% exceed 600 feet.

The deepest recorded well is 1,510 feet. These results fit Aspen’s fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss. Fractures control where water is found, so depth can change sharply from one lot to the next. When comparing bids, ask what footage is included, how casing and grout are handled, and what happens if the hole must continue beyond the planned depth.

sections.heading: Most Aspen wells produce useful flow, but verify the lot
sections.html:
Among the 291 Aspen-area records that report pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute. The middle half is 10.0 to 17.0 gallons per minute. Sixty-seven percent report more than 15 gallons per minute, while 24% fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. Six percent report 1 to 5 gallons per minute, and 2% report less than 1 gallon per minute.

That distribution is encouraging for ordinary household planning, but the yield record is incomplete and a test result is not the same as guaranteed long-term supply. A low-yield well may still work with storage and careful demand management, while a higher-yield result does not replace water-quality testing. Confirm the actual well test, pump size, storage tank, and permitted use before relying on a seller’s description.

sections.heading: Aspen water levels are shallow in the records, not a proven trend
sections.html:
Only 59 permitted wells near Aspen report a static water level, so the water-level sample is much smaller than the depth sample. The reported median depth to water is 41 feet, with the middle half between 14 and 100 feet. In practical terms, many reported wells encountered water relatively close to the surface, but that does not establish the water level on every parcel.

The available facts do not provide a decade-by-decade static-water series, so they do not show a defensible rising or dropping trend. Ask for the well’s static level, pumping level, and test date rather than assuming nearby records apply directly. In fractured rock, water levels and production can depend on local fractures, elevation, recharge, and seasonal conditions.

sections.heading: Aspen’s permit history shows long local drilling experience
sections.html:
Permit records near Aspen reach back to the 1950s and include a newest permit year of 2025. The largest decade in the record is the 1990s, with 410 permits. The 1980s account for 204, the 2000s for 237, and the 2010s for 151. The 2020s account for 103 permits so far in the record.

The most active named drillers are Shelton Drilling Corporation, with 480 records; Steve Shelton Drilling, Inc., with 119; and Collins Drilling Co, with 95. Those records show who has worked in the area, not a guarantee of current availability or performance. Before hiring anyone, check licensing, insurance, references for comparable fractured-rock sites, and the written scope for drilling, casing, grout, testing, and pump installation.

sections.heading: Budget Aspen drilling separately from the finished water system
sections.html:
For Aspen’s fractured mountain bedrock, the cost model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the 127-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $8,300 to $12,700. That is only the hole. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $14,300 to $24,700.

A buyer should treat those figures as planning ranges rather than a fixed quote. Depth beyond the median, difficult access, casing and grout requirements, disposal, electrical distance, and a low-yield design can change the final price. Ask whether the proposal covers a pump test and what is excluded. On a raw lot, also price the access driveway, site development, septic system, and utility routing separately.

sections.heading: Check water quality, dry-hole risk, and septic fit
sections.html:
Aspen records identify 1,554 wells with unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, 39 in the Mancos aquifer, and 22 in alluvial aquifers. The area also has 14 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 129 historic mine features, and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites mapped within about 10 miles. These locations do not prove a problem at a specific parcel, but they are reasons to test instead of assuming well water is safe.

Request a current laboratory test and review nearby mine, cleanup, and septic information. Confirm setbacks and soil suitability for a new septic system before building. Also check the permit’s use: 66% of the records are domestic or household, while other permits serve stock, irrigation, or monitoring purposes. A well permit is not a substitute for confirming the legal household supply and the planned building use.

sections.heading: Use neighboring wells to plan an Aspen purchase
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel’s DWR permit, construction report, pump test, static water level, and water-quality results. Then compare nearby wells rather than relying only on the regional median. The Aspen-area record shows a 127-foot median depth and 15.0-gallon-per-minute median yield, but fractured granite and gneiss can make one lot perform differently from the next.

For a vacant lot, have a licensed driller review access, likely casing and grout, estimated depth, and the consequences of a dry or low-yield hole. Confirm the permit path and any augmentation requirements if the basin or proposed use calls for them. A domestic or exempt household-use well is still subject to its permit conditions and the 35-gallon-per-minute exempt-well pumping limit. Build the well, septic, driveway, and house plan together.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Aspen, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded well depth within 5 miles of Aspen is 127 feet. The middle half runs from 63 to 260 feet. Forty percent are under 100 feet, while 20% are between 300 and 600 feet. The deepest record is 1,510 feet, showing why a local driller should allow for fractured-bedrock variation.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Aspen?
faq.a: The drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the 127-foot median depth, the hole is estimated at $8,300 to $12,700. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $14,300 to $24,700. Access, unusual depth, casing, grout, and low-yield equipment can affect the quote.

faq.q: How much water do Aspen wells produce?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield is 15.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 10.0 to 17.0 gallons per minute. Sixty-seven percent of reported yields exceed 15 gallons per minute. The sample includes only 291 yield reports, so ask for the specific well’s pump test and storage arrangement before planning household demand.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Aspen, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from a permit or regional statistics. Within about 10 miles, records map 14 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 129 historic mine features, and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Request a current laboratory test for the property and investigate nearby mine, cleanup, septic, and land-use history before relying on the water.

faq.q: Are Aspen wells running out of water?
faq.a: The available records do not show a defensible water-level trend because only 59 wells report static water levels and no decade-by-decade series is provided. Those reports have a 41-foot median depth to water, with a middle half from 14 to 100 feet. Verify the individual well’s static and pumping levels, test date, and production history.
